description: TSMC is the world's largest dedicated semiconductor foundry, headquartered in Hsinchu, Taiwan, with a dominant global geographic footprint. In 2025, 74.4% of its US$122.42 billion revenue came from the US, 8.6% from China, 7.9% from Taiwan, 3.9% from Japan, 3.3% from EMEA, and 1.8% from other regions. In 2024, geographic revenue split was North America 70%, China 11%, Asia Pacific (ex-China/Japan) 10%, Japan 5%, and EMEA 4%. The company operates advanced fabs in Taiwan, Arizona (USA), Kumamoto (Japan), and Dresden (Germany), with overseas expansion accelerating its global manufacturing presence. TSMC produces over 12,000 different products for customers worldwide, holds ~70% of the global foundry market share, and manufactures 92% of all logic chips at 10nm or smaller nodes.

revenueGeography.reason: For TSMC, the most recent detailed geographic revenue breakdown available is from the 2025 annual report (filed as part of Q4 2025 consolidated financial statements), which provides revenue by geography in NT dollars and percentages. The 2025 data shows revenue by: United States (74.4%), China (8.6%), Taiwan (7.9%), Japan (3.9%), Europe/Middle East/Africa (3.3%), and Others (1.8%). Total revenue for 2025 was NT$3,809,054,272 thousand. Wikipedia also confirms similar percentages for 2025 (US 68.8%, China 11.5%, Taiwan 9.3%, Japan 5.0%, EMEA 3.6%, Other 1.8%) but the official filing data is used as primary source. The most recent quarterly data (Q1 2026) does not provide a geographic breakdown, so the latest full-year (2025) data is used.

geopoliticalRisks.description: TSMC's headquarters and main foundries are in Taiwan, within easy reach of Chinese missiles. China has longstanding claims on Taiwan. A hot war disrupting TSMC's manufacturing would cause $600B-$1T in annual global financial impact. TSMC's chairman warned an invasion would render TSMC not operable. Over 1,000 Chinese ballistic missiles are positioned as a deterrent.

geopoliticalRisks.riskLabel: US export controls on advanced chips to China
geopoliticalRisks.description: TSMC must comply with US Foreign Direct Product Rule (FDPR) due to US technology in its tools. BIS October 2022/2023 rules and January 2025 rules require TSMC to obtain export licenses for chips using 16nm or below process to global destinations unless conditions are met. TSMC halted shipments to Huawei in Sept 2020. Potential $1B+ penalties from Sophgo/Huawei diversion incident.

geopoliticalRisks.riskLabel: Loss of Chinese market and customer base
geopoliticalRisks.description: US export controls restrict TSMC from selling advanced AI/HPC chips to Chinese customers like Alibaba, Baidu, and Huawei. Huawei was TSMC's second-largest customer before the 2020 ban. China's blocking statute (Jan 2021) entitles Chinese entities to seek civil remedies from multinationals complying with foreign laws. China's antitrust investigations and antidumping probes against US chip firms create retaliatory risk.

geopoliticalRisks.riskLabel: Taiwan's export control entity list expansion
geopoliticalRisks.description: On June 10, 2025, Taiwan added 601 entities from Russia, Pakistan, Iran, Myanmar, and China to its Strategic High-Tech Commodities (SHTC) entity list, including Huawei and SMIC. TSMC must now secure government licenses before exporting to these entities. This could expose Taiwan to WTO litigation from China.

President Trump threatened to place tariffs on all Taiwanese semiconductors and announced intentions for more expansive tariffs. Tariffs on semiconductor imports to the US would increase costs and decrease demand for TSMC's products. Trump's 'reciprocal tariffs' on countries with goods trade deficits create uncertainty.

geopoliticalRisks.riskLabel: CHIPS Act restrictions on China expansion
geopoliticalRisks.description: TSMC's subsidies from the US CHIPS Act prevent the company from expanding manufacturing in China. The Act prohibits companies receiving subsidies from increasing production of chips more advanced than 28nm in China and Russia for 10 years. TSMC's VEU authorization for its Nanjing fab may be terminated in the future.

geopoliticalRisks.riskLabel: US AI Diffusion Rule and licensing requirements
geopoliticalRisks.description: The January 2025 AI Diffusion Rule categorizes countries into three tiers, with only 18 key allies facing no restrictions. TSMC may need export licenses for 16nm or below chips to any global destination. The rule applies to AI model 'weights'. BIS rescinded the rule in May 2025 but uncertainty remains.

Every 1% depreciation of the US dollar against the NT dollar results in an approximately 0.4 percentage point decrease in TSMC's operating margin. TSMC's revenue is largely USD-denominated while costs are partly in NTD, creating significant currency exposure.

geopoliticalRisks.riskLabel: Energy costs and carbon fees in Taiwan
geopoliticalRisks.description: Effective April 1, 2024, TSMC faces a 25% higher electricity tariff rate in Taiwan. TSMC will start paying carbon fees in Taiwan from 2026 under the Climate Change Response Act. TSMC accounts for ~5% of Taiwan's total energy consumption, exceeding Taipei city. Taiwan government secured LNG supply through May 2026 but diversification is ongoing.

Taiwan is seismically active. TSMC recognized ~NT$3B in earthquake losses (net of insurance) in Q2 2024 and ~NT$5.3B in Q1 2025 from earthquakes. TSMC consumed over 150,000 tons of water per day in Hsinchu City in 2024 (~10% of city supply), creating water scarcity risk.

geopoliticalRisks.riskLabel: Arizona fab cost overruns and talent shortages
geopoliticalRisks.description: TSMC stated construction costs for US fabs are 4-5x higher than identical plants in Taiwan, making US-made chips at least 50% more expensive. TSMC warned US talent is insufficient for Arizona fabs, requiring Taiwanese workers temporarily. Gross margin dilution of 2-3% expected from overseas expansion in 2026.

geopoliticalRisks.riskLabel: Middle East conflict driving chemical/gas prices
geopoliticalRisks.description: Geopolitical uncertainty in the Middle East is driving up prices for chemicals and gases used in semiconductor manufacturing. TSMC cited this as a factor in rising component prices. Memory price hikes impact price-sensitive end markets (PC, smartphone). Foxconn called the Middle East war the biggest external challenge in 2026.

China adopted a blocking statute (Jan 2021) allowing Chinese entities to seek civil remedies from multinationals complying with foreign laws. China opened antitrust investigations against Nvidia (Dec 2024) and Qualcomm (Oct 2025), and an antidumping investigation on US analog chips (Sept 2025). China uses export controls on germanium, gallium, and rare earth magnets to retaliate.

geopoliticalRisks.riskLabel: Chinese self-sufficiency eroding TSMC's strategic value
geopoliticalRisks.description: US export controls encourage China to develop domestic advanced chip manufacturing, potentially eliminating Chinese economic dependence on Taiwan. China's Big Fund invested $14.92B (phase 1) and $31.6B (phase 2) in semiconductors. Tax exemptions for Chinese foundries producing <28nm nodes. This erodes Taiwan's 'silicon shield' deterrent.

geopoliticalRisks.riskLabel: Trade secret theft and IP risks
geopoliticalRisks.description: In August 2025, TSMC reported that two current and six former employees had illegally acquired trade secrets related to the 2nm process. TSMC has been entangled in disputes over trade secret theft and industrial espionage with competitors in South Korea and China. Chinese tech enterprises set up head-hunting agencies in Taiwan to poach talent.

In February 2025, Longitude Licensing Ltd. and Marlin Semiconductor Limited filed complaints with the US ITC and US District Court alleging TSMC and its customers infringe five US patents. The ITC instituted an investigation on March 21, 2025.

geopoliticalRisks.riskLabel: Japan export restrictions on semiconductor equipment
geopoliticalRisks.description: Japan listed 23 types of semiconductor technology subject to export restrictions beginning July 23, 2023, including advanced chip manufacturing equipment. The Netherlands restricted sales of ASML's EUV tools to China since 2019 and tightened DUV restrictions in March 2023. These multilateral controls affect TSMC's supply chain.

geopoliticalRisks.riskLabel: Global trade fragmentation and supply chain restructuring
geopoliticalRisks.description: Geopolitical tensions and US tariffs on China are restructuring global supply chains. TSMC adopted a 'China for China' strategy, localizing supply chains in China. The multilateral trade agreements the US has with Japan and the Netherlands do not include Taiwan, leaving TSMC exposed to asymmetric regulatory burdens.
